overview:
Multiple-text codices are bound manuscripts that contain more than one distinct textual work within a single physical volume. In the Jain context, they are a major vehicle for transmitting scripture, commentaries, ritual manuals, hymns, narratives, and scholastic treatises together, often across multiple languages such as Prakrit, Sanskrit, and regional vernaculars. Rather than being random compilations, these codices usually reflect deliberate editorial choices that respond to the needs of monastic communities, lay congregations, and specific ritual or pedagogical settings.

Historically, Jain manuscript culture developed in both palm-leaf and paper formats, with pothī-style manuscripts gradually giving way to codex-style bindings in many regions. As collections grew, scribes and patrons began to copy clusters of related texts into single volumes: for example, a canonical text accompanied by its commentary, or a ritual scripture followed by liturgical hymns and narrative exempla. This practice produced what modern scholarship calls multiple-text manuscripts (MTMs) or multiple-text codices. In catalogues, such codices can be difficult to describe because they combine works of different genres, lengths, and languages, yet they are crucial witnesses to how Jains actually used texts in lived practice.

The functions of multiple-text codices are diverse. Some codices serve as portable liturgical repertoires, gathering hymns (stavan), devotional narratives, and short doctrinal summaries for daily temple or home worship. Others assemble scholastic materials—such as logic, grammar, and doctrinal compendia—used in monastic education. There are also codices that juxtapose canonical or semi-canonical texts with later vernacular retellings, illustrating processes of literary transcreation and the ongoing reinterpretation of authoritative traditions. In many cases, the order of texts within a codex reveals a hierarchy of importance or a ritual sequence, showing how doctrinal instruction, narrative illustration, and devotional practice were woven together.

From a technical perspective, multiple-text codices raise important questions for philology and manuscript studies. They complicate the notion of a single "work" by embedding it in a curated ensemble, and they highlight the role of scribes, patrons, and local communities in shaping textual transmission. Language choice within codices—Prakrit for early canonical material, Sanskrit for scholastic treatises, and Gujarati, Rajasthani, or early Hindi for vernacular hymns and stories—reflects the multilingual reality of Jain communities. Codices also preserve canonized assemblages (stable combinations copied repeatedly) alongside more dynamic collections that vary from one manuscript to another. For historians of Jainism, these codices are therefore not only containers of texts but also records of ritual, pedagogical, and social priorities.

In the broader South Asian manuscript landscape, Jain multiple-text codices participate in a pan-Indian phenomenon of compiling diverse works into single volumes, yet they exhibit distinctive features. The strong emphasis on ethical instruction, nonviolence, and ascetic ideals, combined with rich narrative and devotional literature, gives Jain codices a particular thematic profile. Their careful colophons often record donors, copying dates in Vikrama or Śaka eras, and the intended use of the manuscript, allowing scholars to trace networks of patronage and circulation. Modern cataloguing and digitization projects continue to uncover new multiple-text codices in temple libraries and private collections, making them central to reconstructing Jain intellectual and ritual history.

Because multiple-text codices reflect lived practice rather than abstract theory, they must be read with attention to both their internal structure and their external context. The juxtaposition of texts can signal interpretive relationships, ritual sequences, or pedagogical progressions. At the same time, the physical features of the codex—script, illumination, marginalia, and signs of use—offer clues about how often and by whom it was read. For students of Jainism, engaging with these codices provides a more holistic view of the tradition, showing how canonical doctrine, commentary, narrative, and devotion coexisted within the same material object and within the same community life.

primary_sources.title: Kalpasūtra with Kālaka narrative in a multiple-text codex
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu (Kalpasūtra); Kālaka story anonymous
primary_sources.original_text:
कल्लणं कल्लणं कल्लणं
जिणवरं वंदामि महावीरं।
primary_sources.transliteration:
kallaṇaṁ kallaṇaṁ kallaṇaṁ
jiṇavaraṁ vandāmi mahāvīraṁ.
primary_sources.translation:
Auspicious, auspicious, auspicious—
I bow to the Jina, Lord Mahāvīra.
primary_sources.notes: Many Śvetāmbara mūrti-pūjaka codices combine the Kalpasūtra, a key ritual and biographical text recited especially during Paryuṣaṇa, with the narrative of Kālaka and related hymns. This combination forms a classic example of a multiple-text codex in which a semi-canonical text is accompanied by narrative and devotional material that elaborates its themes. The presence of metrical verses like the one cited here, often in Sanskrit or mixed Prakrit, illustrates how liturgical praise is interwoven with biographical and doctrinal content. Scholarly discussions of such codices and their functions can be found in Nalini Balbir, “Functions of Multiple-Text Manuscripts in India: The Jain Case,” in The Emergence of Multiple-Text Manuscripts (2019), which analyzes how the Kalpasūtra–Kālaka pairing became a canonized assemblage within Jain manuscript culture.

primary_sources.title: Harley 415: Gujarati hymns and narrative poems codex
primary_sources.author: Multiple anonymous Jain authors
primary_sources.original_text:
श्री जिनेश्वर प्रभुने वंदन करूँँ,
दया धर्मना मार्गे चालूँँ।
primary_sources.transliteration:
śrī jineśvara prabhune vandan karū̃,
dayā dharmnā mārge chālū̃.
primary_sources.translation:
I bow to Lord Jineśvara,
may I walk on the path of compassionate dharma.
primary_sources.notes: British Library Harley 415, dated V.S. 1673 (1616 CE), is often cited as one of the earliest Jain multiple-text codices to enter a European collection. It contains a collection of Gujarati hymns (stavan) and narrative poems of varying length, all in a vernacular register. This codex exemplifies a monolingual multiple-text manuscript intended for daily religious practice, offering a repertoire of songs and stories suitable for lay devotion. Its structure shows how multiple short works were copied together to form a practical devotional anthology. Nalini Balbir’s study of Jain multiple-text manuscripts highlights Harley 415 as evidence for the popularity of vernacular MTMs and their role in shaping communal worship and cultural memory.

primary_sources.title: Didactic Prakrit verses in a scholastic multiple-text codex
primary_sources.author: Anonymous Jain teacher (Prakrit gnomic verses)
primary_sources.original_text:
अहिंसा परमो धम्मो,
सव्वे जीवो दया वहे।
primary_sources.transliteration:
ahiṁsā paramo dhammo,
savve jīvo dayā vahe.
primary_sources.translation:
Nonviolence is the supreme dharma;
let compassion flow toward all living beings.
primary_sources.notes: Scholastic multiple-text codices often combine doctrinal summaries, logical treatises, and gnomic verses in Prakrit or Sanskrit. The cited verse, in a common Prakrit formulation, encapsulates the central Jain ethic of ahiṁsā and universal compassion. In many codices, such verses appear alongside prose expositions, commentaries, and even grammatical notes, forming a pedagogical ensemble for monastic students. The coexistence of brief didactic stanzas with more elaborate scholastic works demonstrates how multiple-text codices functioned as teaching tools, integrating memorisable aphorisms with systematic doctrinal instruction. Modern scholarship on Jain literary transcreation, such as the volume "Literary Transcreation as a Jain Practice" (ed. Eva De Clercq et al., 2025), shows how these didactic units were repeatedly reworked and embedded in new codical contexts, further enriching the MTM tradition.

misconceptions.myth: Multiple-text codices are random compilations of unrelated works bound together without any organizing principle.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain manuscript culture, multiple-text codices usually reflect deliberate editorial and ritual choices. Texts are selected and ordered to serve specific functions—such as festival recitation, daily devotion, or monastic study—and often form stable, canonized assemblages that are copied repeatedly. The combinations of texts, their sequence, and their languages reveal coherent patterns rather than arbitrary aggregation.

misconceptions.myth: Only canonical scriptures are worthy of inclusion in multiple-text codices; vernacular hymns and narratives are secondary additions.
misconceptions.reality: Many Jain multiple-text codices are built primarily around vernacular hymns, narratives, and didactic poems, especially in Gujarati, Rajasthani, or early Hindi. These works are central to lay devotion and community identity, and their inclusion in codices shows that lived religious practice values them alongside, and sometimes even above, more formal canonical texts. The codices thus preserve a rich spectrum of genres that together express Jain doctrine and devotion.

misconceptions.myth: The presence of several texts in one codex means that each text circulated independently and the codex is merely a convenient storage device.
misconceptions.reality: While individual works may have independent histories, their juxtaposition in a multiple-text codex often creates new interpretive and ritual relationships. A narrative placed after a doctrinal treatise can function as an exemplum; hymns following a scripture can guide its liturgical use. The codex is therefore not just a neutral container but an active medium that shapes how texts are read, remembered, and performed within Jain communities.
